profile.reading:
Per CoreSite's own facility page, this building, AT1, is located at 55 Marietta St. NW, Atlanta, GA 30303, in downtown Atlanta. CoreSite publishes 62,000-plus square feet for this building, consistent across the main facility page and the operator's spec-sheet landing page. No MW capacity or opening year is stated. CoreSite lists SOC 1 Type 2, SOC 2 Type 2, ISO 27001, NIST 800-53, PCI DSS, and HIPAA compliance for its facilities generally.

CoreSite is a subsidiary of American Tower Corporation (NYSE: AMT), which completed its acquisition of CoreSite in late 2021; Stonepeak Partners LP separately acquired roughly 29% of American Tower's US data center business in July 2022, later increased to about 36%. CoreSite's own site describes a total portfolio of 30 data centers across 11 US markets, including Atlanta, totaling more than 4.8 million square feet, with more than 44,000 customer interconnections and 500-plus connected network providers. Georgia has separately drawn intense hyperscale investment, with Georgia Power forecasting demand growth from roughly 400 megawatts to nearly 10,000 megawatts of data center-driven load and the state offering a $296 million sales tax exemption program for large data center projects, per Atlanta Journal-Constitution and Atlanta Tech News reporting, a very different scale of activity than this downtown interconnection-focused CoreSite building represents.

American Tower reported record leasing at CoreSite driving stronger-than-expected second-quarter 2026 results, projecting data-center segment revenue of $1.20 billion to $1.22 billion for full-year 2026, roughly 14.9% growth at the midpoint, and raising its full-year outlook on the strength of that performance; the company also budgeted approximately $695 million in data-center development spending for 2026, funding continued build-out across CoreSite's 11-market US portfolio.

profile.research_note: [batch narration moved out of reading 2026-09-02] This CoreSite facility is in one of the company confirmed operating markets. Wikipedia coverage states that as of June 2022 CoreSite operated 27 data center facilities across 10 markets totaling over 4.6 million net rentable square feet, with key locations including Boston, Chicago, Denver, Los Angeles, Miami, New York City, Northern Virginia, San Francisco/San Jose, Santa Clara, Atlanta, Orlando, and Washington, D.C. In May 2007 the company acquired Chicago properties as part of a wider expansion. CoreSite began operating a Washington, D.C. facility in August 2005, one of its earliest East Coast sites after founding in 2001 as CRG West. CoreSite rebranded from CRG West to CoreSite in June 2009, went public in September 2010, and was acquired by American Tower in December 2021. This specific market was confirmed as an active CoreSite location, but no market specific acquisition date or building history beyond the general company timeline was located in available sourcing this session.

reading.body:
CoreSite AT1 publishes no power consumption figure, making its compute capacity invisible to AI scaling analysis despite occupying 62,000 square feet in downtown Atlanta.

The facility holds six security certifications that qualify it for regulated workloads in finance, payments, and healthcare. SOC 1 Type 2, SOC 2 Type 2, ISO 27001, NIST 800-53, PCI DSS, and HIPAA are not AI-specific, but they permit AI training and inference within the compliance boundaries that regulated industries increasingly require. This matters because AI workloads in banking, insurance, and pharmaceuticals must often run in certified environments, and AT1 can host them.

Georgia contains 33 mapped data center facilities in this dataset, but only two publish megawatt figures, totaling 42 MW. AT1 does not report its power draw, so the true installed capacity across the state is unknown. This opacity is the binding problem for understanding whether Georgia's infrastructure can support AI scaling. Floor area alone cannot estimate power demand without a watts-per-square-foot figure the operator has not supplied. AT1 may house significant compute or minimal workload. The dataset cannot distinguish between the two.
